title: Pair Sum Indices
prompt:
You are given a list of integers nums and an integer target. Exactly one pair of distinct positions i < j satisfies nums[i] + nums[j] == target. Return that pair as a list [i, j] with i < j.

You may not use the same position twice. Aim for a single pass over the list.

Example:
  pair_sum_indices([4, 9, 1, 6], 7) -> [2, 3]   (1 + 6 = 7)

title: Balanced Brackets
prompt:
Given a string s made only of the characters ( ) [ ] { }, decide whether the brackets are balanced. A string is balanced when every opening bracket is closed by the same kind of bracket, and brackets close in the reverse order they were opened. The empty string is balanced.

Return True or False.

Example:
  is_balanced("{[()]}()") -> True
  is_balanced("([)]") -> False

title: Group Anagrams
prompt:
Given a list of lowercase words, group together the words that are anagrams of each other (they use exactly the same letters with the same counts). Return a list of groups, where each group is a list of words.

The order of the groups and the order of words inside each group do not matter. Every input word must appear in exactly one group (duplicates stay duplicates).

Example:
  group_anagrams(["listen", "pots", "silent", "stop", "tops", "cat"])
  -> [["listen", "silent"], ["pots", "stop", "tops"], ["cat"]]   (any order)

title: Smallest Covering Window
prompt:
Given two strings s and t, find the shortest contiguous substring of s that contains every character of t, counting multiplicity (if t has two 'a's, the window needs at least two 'a's). Return that substring. If no such window exists, return the empty string "". When several shortest windows exist, return the one that starts earliest.

Example:
  min_cover_window("XADOBECODEBANC", "ABC") -> "BANC"
  min_cover_window("a", "aa") -> ""

title: Palindrome After Cleanup
prompt:
Given a string s, decide whether it reads the same forwards and backwards after you ignore every character that is not a letter or digit and treat uppercase and lowercase letters as equal. A string with no letters or digits counts as a palindrome.

Try to solve it with two pointers and O(1) extra space.

Example:
  is_clean_palindrome("Was it a car, or a cat I saw?") -> True
  is_clean_palindrome("race a car") -> False

title: Search a Rotated Sorted List
prompt:
A list of distinct integers was sorted in ascending order and then rotated at some unknown pivot (for example [1,2,3,4,5,6] might become [4,5,6,1,2,3]). Given this list nums and a value target, return the index of target in nums, or -1 if it is absent.

Your solution should run in O(log n) time.

Example:
  search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3], 2) -> 4
  search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3], 7) -> -1

title: Reverse a Linked List
prompt:
You are given the head of a singly linked list built from ListNode objects (each has a val and a next). Reverse the list in place and return the new head. An empty list is represented by None.

Example:
  1 -> 2 -> 3 -> None   becomes   3 -> 2 -> 1 -> None

title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists
prompt:
You are given the heads of two singly linked lists (ListNode objects), each already sorted in non-decreasing order. Splice their nodes together into one sorted list and return its head. Either input may be None (empty).

Example:
  a: 1 -> 4 -> 6     b: 2 -> 4 -> 9
  result: 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 4 -> 6 -> 9

title: Binary Tree Height
prompt:
Given the root of a binary tree made of TreeNode objects (val, left, right), return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to any leaf. An empty tree (root is None) has height 0, and a single node has height 1.

Example:
        3
       / \
      9   20
         /  \
        15   7
  tree_height(root) -> 3

title: Check Binary Search Tree
prompt:
Given the root of a binary tree (TreeNode objects), decide whether it is a valid binary search tree. In a valid BST, for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly less than the node's value and all values in its right subtree are strictly greater. An empty tree is valid.

Note: comparing each node only with its direct children is not enough.

Example:
      5
     / \
    3   8
       / \
      4   9
  is_bst(root) -> False   (4 sits in the right subtree of 5 but is smaller than 5)

title: Count the Islands
prompt:
You are given a rectangular grid as a list of strings, where '#' is land and '.' is water. An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically (not diagonally). Return the number of islands. The grid may be empty.

Do not assume you can modify the input in place (strings are immutable anyway).

Example:
  count_islands([
      "##..#",
      "#...#",
      "..#..",
      "....#",
  ]) -> 4

title: Build Order
prompt:
There are n tasks labeled 0 to n-1. You are given a list of dependencies, where each dependency [a, b] means task b must be finished before task a can start. Return a list containing all n tasks in an order that respects every dependency. If no such order exists (the dependencies contain a cycle), return an empty list.

Any valid order is accepted.

Example:
  build_order(4, [[1, 0], [2, 0], [3, 1], [3, 2]]) -> [0, 1, 2, 3]   (or [0, 2, 1, 3])
  build_order(2, [[0, 1], [1, 0]]) -> []

title: Most Frequent K Values
prompt:
Given a list of integers nums and an integer k, return the k values that occur most often in nums. The answer is guaranteed to be unique (there are no ties at the k-th position). The returned values may be in any order.

Try to do better than sorting all distinct values when k is small, for example with a heap.

Example:
  top_k_frequent([5, 5, 5, 2, 2, 9], 2) -> [5, 2]   (any order)

title: Combine Overlapping Ranges
prompt:
You are given a list of closed ranges, each written as [start, end] with start <= end. Merge every group of ranges that overlap or touch (share an endpoint) and return the resulting list of ranges sorted by start. The input is not necessarily sorted.

Example:
  merge_ranges([[8, 10], [1, 3], [2, 6], [15, 18], [18, 20]])
  -> [[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 20]]

title: Edit Distance
prompt:
Given two strings a and b, return the minimum number of single-character edits needed to turn a into b. The allowed edits are: insert one character, delete one character, or replace one character with another.

Example:
  edit_distance("kitten", "sitting") -> 3
  edit_distance("", "abc") -> 3

title: Target Sum Combinations
prompt:
Given a list of distinct positive integers candidates and a positive integer target, return every unique combination of candidates whose values sum to target. Each candidate may be used any number of times. Two combinations are the same if they use the same values the same number of times, regardless of order.

Return a list of combinations; the order of combinations and the order within each combination do not matter. If none exist, return an empty list.

Example:
  sum_combinations([2, 3, 5], 8) -> [[2, 2, 2, 2], [2, 3, 3], [3, 5]]   (any order)

title: Count Queen Placements
prompt:
On an n x n chessboard, you want to place n queens so that no two queens attack each other (no two share a row, a column, or a diagonal). Return the number of distinct ways to do this. For n = 0, return 1 (the empty placement).

Example:
  count_queen_placements(4) -> 2
  count_queen_placements(3) -> 0

title: Prefix Tree
prompt:
Implement a class PrefixTree that stores lowercase words and supports:

  insert(word)       add word to the tree
  contains(word)     return True if word was inserted exactly, else False
  has_prefix(prefix) return True if any inserted word starts with prefix, else False
  count_prefix(prefix) return how many inserted words start with prefix (inserting the same word twice counts once)

The empty string is a prefix of every word. Build it as a trie of nodes rather than scanning a list of words.

Example:
  t = PrefixTree()
  t.insert("card"); t.insert("care")
  t.contains("car") -> False
  t.has_prefix("car") -> True
  t.count_prefix("car") -> 2
tests:
def test_example():
    t = PrefixTree()
    t.insert("card")
    t.insert("care")
    assert t.contains("car") is False
    assert t.has_prefix("car") is True
    assert t.count_prefix("car") == 2

def test_exact_word():
    t = PrefixTree()
    t.insert("car")
    t.insert("card")
    assert t.contains("car") is True
    assert t.contains("card") is True
    assert t.contains("ca") is False

def test_missing_prefix():
    t = PrefixTree()
    t.insert("apple")
    assert t.has_prefix("apx") is False
    assert t.count_prefix("b") == 0
    assert t.contains("applesauce") is False

def test_duplicates_and_empty_prefix():
    t = PrefixTree()
    for w in ["a", "ab", "ab", "abc", "b"]:
        t.insert(w)
    assert t.count_prefix("") == 4
    assert t.count_prefix("ab") == 2
    assert t.has_prefix("") is True

def test_many_words():
    t = PrefixTree()
    for i in range(3000):
        t.insert("w" + str(i))
    assert t.count_prefix("w1") == 1111
    assert t.contains("w2999") is True

title: Least Recently Used Cache
prompt:
Implement a class LRUCache with a fixed positive capacity that supports:

  get(key)        return the value stored for key, or -1 if key is absent. A successful get counts as a use.
  put(key, value) store value under key (overwriting any existing value; this counts as a use). If inserting a new key would exceed capacity, first evict the key that was used least recently.

Both operations should run in O(1) average time.

Example:
  c = LRUCache(2)
  c.put(1, 10); c.put(2, 20)
  c.get(1)      -> 10
  c.put(3, 30)  # evicts key 2
  c.get(2)      -> -1
tests:
def test_example():
    c = LRUCache(2)
    c.put(1, 10)
    c.put(2, 20)
    assert c.get(1) == 10
    c.put(3, 30)
    assert c.get(2) == -1
    assert c.get(3) == 30

def test_missing_key():
    c = LRUCache(1)
    assert c.get(99) == -1

def test_overwrite_refreshes():
    c = LRUCache(2)
    c.put(1, 1)
    c.put(2, 2)
    c.put(1, 100)
    c.put(3, 3)
    assert c.get(1) == 100
    assert c.get(2) == -1

def test_capacity_one():
    c = LRUCache(1)
    c.put(1, 1)
    c.put(2, 2)
    assert c.get(1) == -1
    assert c.get(2) == 2

def test_many_ops_fast():
    c = LRUCache(1000)
    for i in range(50000):
        c.put(i, i * 2)
        c.get(i - 500)
    assert c.get(49999) == 99998
    assert c.get(10) == -1

title: Trapped Rainwater
prompt:
You are given a list of non-negative integers heights describing an elevation map, where each bar has width 1. After it rains, water collects in the dips between taller bars. Return the total units of water that are trapped. Water spills off both ends of the map.

Aim for O(n) time; O(1) extra space is possible with two pointers.

Example:
  trapped_water([3, 0, 2, 0, 4]) -> 7
  trapped_water([0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]) -> 6

title: URL Shortener
prompt:
You are building a service that turns long URLs into short links (e.g. sho.rt/aZ3k9Q) and redirects visitors to the original URL.

Functional requirements:
- Create a short link for a long URL, optionally with a custom alias and an expiry date.
- Redirect a short link to its original URL with low latency.
- Show basic click counts per link to the creator.

Scale:
- 100M new links per month; read:write ratio around 100:1.
- Links retained for 5 years by default.
- Redirect p99 latency target under 50 ms.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you generate short codes so they are unique, short, and not trivially guessable? How long must the code be?
2. What storage would you use and how large does it get over 5 years?
3. How do you serve redirects at peak read load, and should you return 301 or 302?
4. How do you record click counts without slowing down redirects?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Writes: 100M/month is about 40 writes/s average, ~200/s peak.
- Reads: ~4,000/s average, ~20k/s peak.
- 5 years = 6B links. At ~500 bytes per row that is ~3 TB.
- Base62 with 7 chars = 62^7 = 3.5 trillion codes, ample headroom.

API
- POST /links {long_url, alias?, expires_at?} -> {code, short_url}
- GET /{code} -> 302 Location: long_url
- GET /links/{code}/stats -> {clicks, by_day}

DATA MODEL
- links(code PK, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at)
- A key-value or wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) fits: single-key lookups, no joins.

CODE GENERATION
- Option A: a global counter handed out in ranges (each app server leases a block of 10k IDs from a coordinator), then base62-encode. No collisions, but sequential codes are guessable; mitigate by passing the ID through a reversible bijective scramble (e.g. a Feistel permutation) before encoding.
- Option B: random 7-char codes with a conditional insert (put-if-absent) and retry on collision. Simple and unguessable; collision rate is tiny while the space is mostly empty.
- Hashing the long URL (MD5 then truncate) gives dedup but needs collision handling and leaks equality.

READ PATH
- CDN or edge cache, then Redis cache (LRU, hot links follow a power law), then the database.
- 302 keeps analytics accurate because browsers re-request every time; 301 is cached by browsers and cuts load but you lose click visibility. Most services use 302.

ANALYTICS
- Redirect handler emits a click event to a queue (Kafka) asynchronously; a stream job aggregates counts per code per day into a separate store. Never do a synchronous counter increment on the hot path.

TRADE-OFFS AND PITFALLS
- Custom aliases share the namespace; reserve them with the same conditional insert.
- Expired links: lazy check on read plus a background cleanup job.
- Abuse: scan new URLs against malware/phishing lists, rate limit creation per user/IP.
- Do not use a single auto-increment DB as the only ID source; it becomes a write bottleneck and a single point of failure.

title: Pastebin
prompt:
Design a service where users paste text (code snippets, logs) and get a shareable link. Pastes can be public, unlisted, or private, and may expire.

Functional requirements:
- Create a paste up to 10 MB with optional syntax language, visibility, and expiry (10 min, 1 day, 1 month, never).
- View a paste by link; raw view for download.
- Expired pastes must stop being viewable promptly.

Scale:
- 5M new pastes per day, average size 10 KB.
- 50M paste views per day, heavily skewed toward recent pastes.

Questions to answer:
1. Where do you store paste content versus metadata, and why?
2. How much storage do you need per year?
3. How do you implement expiry efficiently?
4. How do you keep reads fast and cheap for viral pastes?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Writes: 5M/day = ~60/s average.
- Reads: 50M/day = ~600/s average, a few thousand per second at peak.
- Storage: 5M x 10 KB = 50 GB/day, ~18 TB/year of content. Metadata is ~200 bytes per paste, ~365 GB/year.

API
- POST /pastes {content, language?, visibility, ttl} -> {id, url}
- GET /pastes/{id} -> metadata plus rendered content
- GET /raw/{id} -> plain text

DATA MODEL
- Metadata in a relational or KV store: pastes(id PK, owner_id, object_key, size, language, visibility, created_at, expires_at).
- Content in object storage (S3) keyed by id. Blobs do not belong in the database: cheaper, scales independently, and can be served via CDN.
- Small pastes (under a few KB) could be inlined in the metadata row to save an extra hop; a reasonable optimization.

ARCHITECTURE
- Stateless API servers behind a load balancer.
- ID generation: random 8-char base62 with put-if-absent, or a Snowflake-style ID encoded.
- Uploads: for large pastes, issue a pre-signed URL so clients upload directly to object storage.
- Reads: CDN in front of /raw for public and unlisted pastes; Redis for hot metadata.

EXPIRY
- Check expires_at on every read and return 404 if past; this guarantees correctness regardless of cleanup lag.
- Background sweeper deletes expired metadata (indexed by expires_at) and object storage lifecycle rules or explicit deletes remove blobs.
- Set CDN cache TTL to min(default, time until expiry) so expired content is not served from the edge.

PRIVACY
- Private pastes require auth and must never be cached publicly at the CDN; use signed short-lived URLs.
- Unlisted means unguessable IDs; do not use sequential IDs.

PITFALLS
- Rendering syntax highlighting server-side on every view is wasteful; do it client-side or cache rendered HTML.
- Abuse: rate limit anonymous creation, scan for leaked secrets and malware.
- Content-addressed dedup (hash of content) saves space but complicates deletion; reference count if used.

title: Unique ID Generator (Snowflake-style)
prompt:
Many services in your company need globally unique 64-bit IDs for rows, events, and messages. A single database sequence can no longer keep up.

Functional requirements:
- Generate IDs that are unique across all data centers without coordination per request.
- IDs should be roughly sortable by creation time.
- IDs must fit in a signed 64-bit integer.

Scale:
- Peak 500k IDs per second globally across 5 data centers.
- Generation latency under 1 ms; the service must survive the loss of any single node.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you lay out the 64 bits, and how long will the scheme last?
2. How are worker/machine IDs assigned and kept unique?
3. What happens when a machine's clock moves backward?
4. Should ID generation be a network service or an embedded library?
notes:
BIT LAYOUT (classic)
- 1 sign bit (always 0).
- 41 bits timestamp in ms since a custom epoch: 2^41 ms is about 69 years.
- 10 bits worker ID: 1,024 workers (could split 5 DC + 5 machine).
- 12 bits sequence: 4,096 IDs per ms per worker, i.e. ~4M/s per worker.
- 500k/s globally is easy; even a handful of workers cover it.

GENERATION ALGORITHM
- now = current ms. If now == last_ms, sequence++; if sequence overflows 4,095, spin until next ms. If now > last_ms, reset sequence to 0 (or a random small value to spread shard keys).
- ID = (now - epoch) << 22 | worker_id << 12 | sequence.

WORKER ID ASSIGNMENT
- Lease from ZooKeeper/etcd with an ephemeral node, or from a DB table with a lease TTL.
- Statically configured IDs work for small fleets but are error-prone with autoscaling.
- Two processes with the same worker ID will produce duplicates; leases must be fenced (process stops generating if it loses its lease).

CLOCK SKEW
- Run NTP with slewing, not stepping.
- If the clock goes backward by a small amount, wait until it catches up to last_ms; if by a large amount, refuse to generate and alert.
- Persist last_ms periodically so a restart after a backward jump does not reuse timestamps.

SERVICE VS LIBRARY
- Library: zero network hop, highest throughput, but every process needs a worker ID (exhausts 1,024 quickly in large fleets).
- Service: fewer worker IDs, centralized control, but adds a network hop and availability dependency; clients can batch-fetch IDs.

TRADE-OFFS
- Only k-sortable: IDs from different workers within the same ms are not strictly ordered.
- IDs reveal creation time and approximate volume; do not expose them where that matters.
- Alternatives: UUIDv4 (128-bit, no ordering, bad for B-tree locality), UUIDv7 (128-bit, time ordered, no coordination), DB range allocation (ticket server handing out blocks).

PITFALLS
- Monotonically increasing keys create a hot last partition in range-sharded stores; consider hashing for the shard key.
- Forgetting sequence overflow handling under bursts.

title: API Rate Limiter
prompt:
Your public API platform needs a rate limiter that protects backend services and enforces per-customer quotas.

Functional requirements:
- Limit requests per API key with configurable rules (e.g. 100 req/s burst, 10k req/hour).
- Different limits per endpoint and per plan tier.
- Return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header when a client is over limit.
- Limits must apply across a fleet of gateway servers, not per server.

Scale:
- 1M active API keys, 2M requests/s at peak across 300 gateway nodes in 3 regions.
- The limiter may add at most 2 ms p99 latency.

Questions to answer:
1. Which algorithm would you use (fixed window, sliding log, sliding window counter, token bucket) and why?
2. Where does limiter state live and how do you keep the check atomic?
3. What do you do if the limiter's state store is unavailable?
4. How do you handle limits across multiple regions?
notes:
ALGORITHMS
- Fixed window counter: cheap, but allows 2x burst at window edges.
- Sliding log: exact, but stores every timestamp; memory heavy.
- Sliding window counter: weighted blend of current and previous window counts; near-exact, two counters per key. Good default for per-hour quotas.
- Token bucket: stores tokens and last_refill; natural fit for burst plus sustained rate. Good default for per-second limits.

STATE AND ATOMICITY
- Central Redis cluster sharded by api_key. 2M req/s is fine across tens of shards.
- Make check-and-decrement atomic with a Lua script (read tokens, refill by elapsed time, decrement if possible, set TTL) to avoid read-modify-write races.
- Key: rl:{api_key}:{rule_id}. TTL equal to window length so idle keys expire.
- Memory: 1M keys x few rules x ~100 bytes = a few hundred MB.

REDUCING LATENCY AND LOAD
- Co-locate Redis with gateways in each region.
- Local pre-aggregation: each gateway keeps an in-memory bucket and syncs with Redis every N ms or every M requests. Trades exactness for far fewer round trips.
- Rules cached locally in each gateway, refreshed from a config service.

FAILURE MODE
- Fail open (allow traffic) when Redis is unreachable, combined with a coarse local per-node limit as a safety net. Failing closed turns a limiter outage into a full API outage.
- Circuit breaker around Redis calls with a tight timeout (about 1 ms).

MULTI-REGION
- Option A: per-region limits (global limit divided by regions or weighted by traffic). Simple, slightly inaccurate.
- Option B: async replication of counters between regions; accept short-term overshoot.
- Strict global consistency would need cross-region round trips; usually not worth it.

RESPONSE
- 429 with Retry-After, plus X-RateLimit-Limit, -Remaining, -Reset headers.

PITFALLS
- Limiting by IP behind NAT punishes many users; prefer API key or user ID.
- Clock differences between gateways when computing windows; use Redis server time inside the script.
- Hot keys from one huge customer; split their bucket across sub-keys or use local aggregation.

title: Real-Time Game Leaderboard
prompt:
A mobile game wants global and friends-only leaderboards that update as players finish matches.

Functional requirements:
- Submit a score after each match; a player's leaderboard score is their best score in the current season.
- Show the top 100 players globally.
- Show a player's own rank and the 10 players above and below them.
- Seasons reset monthly; past season results stay viewable.

Scale:
- 50M monthly active players, 5M daily active.
- 20k score submissions/s at peak; 50k leaderboard reads/s.

Questions to answer:
1. What data structure gives you rank lookups efficiently?
2. How do you store and shard 50M players' scores?
3. How do you serve friends leaderboards?
4. How do you handle season resets and ties?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 50M entries x ~50 bytes in a sorted set is ~2.5-5 GB in memory: fits on one large Redis node, though you want replicas for reads.
- 20k writes/s and 50k reads/s are within a single Redis primary plus read replicas.

CORE STRUCTURE
- Redis sorted set per season: ZADD lb:{season} GT score player_id (GT keeps the best score only).
- Top 100: ZREVRANGE lb:{season} 0 99 WITHSCORES, O(log N + 100).
- My rank: ZREVRANK lb:{season} player_id, O(log N).
- Neighbors: ZREVRANGE with rank-10 to rank+10.

API
- POST /scores {player_id, match_id, score}
- GET /leaderboard/top?season=
- GET /leaderboard/me?season=&window=10
- GET /leaderboard/friends?season=

DURABILITY
- Redis is the serving index, not the source of truth. Write every match result to a durable DB (match_results table) first, publish an event, and have a consumer update Redis. You can rebuild the sorted set from the DB.
- Make updates idempotent by match_id.

FRIENDS LEADERBOARD
- Friend lists are small (typically under 500). Fetch friend IDs, then ZMSCORE on the global set and sort in the app. No separate sorted set per user needed.

SCALING BEYOND ONE NODE
- If the set outgrows a node, shard by score range (each shard holds a band of scores, rank = local rank + count in higher shards) or keep exact top-N in Redis and give approximate rank for the long tail using a score histogram (e.g. "top 12%"). Most players do not need exact rank 31,402,117.

SEASONS AND TIES
- New key per season: lb:2026-10. Old seasons snapshot to the DB / object storage and expire from Redis.
- Ties: encode a tiebreaker into the score, e.g. score x 2^20 + (max_ts - achieved_ts) so earlier achievers rank higher; or accept equal rank.

PITFALLS
- Cheating: validate scores server-side, rate limit submissions, anomaly detection.
- Treating Redis as the only copy of the data.
- Re-sorting in a SQL database on every read (ORDER BY score with OFFSET) does not scale for rank queries.

title: Notification Service
prompt:
Build a central notification platform that other teams call to send push, email, and SMS messages to users.

Functional requirements:
- Producers send a notification request (user, template, channels, priority).
- Respect user preferences (opt-outs per channel and category, quiet hours).
- Support scheduled sends and bulk campaigns to millions of users.
- Track delivery status per message and per channel.

Scale:
- 300M registered users; 1B notifications/day, with marketing campaigns causing 10x spikes.
- Transactional messages (OTP codes, password resets) must be delivered within seconds even during campaigns.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you structure the pipeline from API to third-party providers (APNs, FCM, email/SMS vendors)?
2. How do you prevent transactional messages from being delayed by bulk traffic?
3. How do you avoid sending duplicates while handling retries?
4. How do you deal with provider rate limits and outages?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 1B/day = ~12k/s average, 100k+/s during campaign spikes.
- Status records: 1B x ~200 bytes = 200 GB/day; keep hot for 30 days in a wide-column store, archive the rest.

API
- POST /notify {idempotency_key, user_id | segment_id, template_id, params, channels, priority, send_at?} -> {notification_id}
- GET /notifications/{id}/status

PIPELINE
- API service validates, writes the request record, and enqueues to Kafka.
- Fan-out workers expand segments into per-user tasks (campaigns), in batches.
- Preference/enrichment service: checks opt-outs, quiet hours, frequency caps; resolves device tokens, emails, phone numbers; renders the template.
- Per-channel queues (push, email, sms) consumed by channel senders that call providers.
- Delivery receipts and provider webhooks update the status store.
- Scheduler: store send_at items in a time-indexed table, a poller promotes due items into the queue.

PRIORITY ISOLATION
- Separate topics/queues and dedicated worker pools per priority. Transactional traffic never sits behind a 50M-message campaign.
- Campaigns are throttled at the fan-out stage.

DEDUP AND RETRIES
- Idempotency key from the producer, stored with a unique constraint; repeat requests return the original ID.
- Per-delivery key (notification_id + channel + recipient). Senders check-and-set in Redis before calling the provider.
- At-least-once queues mean exactly-once delivery is impossible end-to-end; aim for effectively-once via dedup, and accept rare duplicates on provider timeouts.
- Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; dead-letter queue after N attempts.

PROVIDERS
- Per-provider token-bucket rate limiting in senders.
- Multiple vendors per channel (two SMS providers) with health-based failover.
- Remove invalid device tokens when APNs/FCM report them unregistered.

PITFALLS
- Checking preferences only at enqueue time; a user who opts out during a long campaign should still be honored at send time.
- Time zones for quiet hours and scheduled campaigns.
- Unbounded retries amplifying a provider outage.

title: Social Media News Feed
prompt:
Design the home feed for a social network where users follow others and see their posts.

Functional requirements:
- Users publish posts (text, images).
- The home feed shows posts from followed accounts, newest first (ranking can come later), with infinite scroll.
- New posts should appear in followers' feeds within a few seconds.

Scale:
- 500M daily active users; average user follows 200 accounts; some celebrities have 100M followers.
- 50M new posts/day; 10B feed reads/day.

Questions to answer:
1. Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, or a hybrid? Justify with the numbers.
2. What is stored in the feed cache and how big is it?
3. How do you handle celebrity accounts?
4. How does pagination work when new posts keep arriving?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Posts: 50M/day = ~600/s, peak ~2k/s.
- Feed reads: 10B/day = ~115k/s, peak ~300k/s. Reads dominate.
- Average fan-out: if average follower count is ~200, 50M posts x 200 = 10B feed inserts/day (~115k/s).

API
- POST /posts {text, media_ids}
- GET /feed?cursor=&limit=20 -> {items, next_cursor}

DATA
- posts(post_id Snowflake, author_id, content, media_refs, created_at) in a sharded store keyed by post_id.
- follows(follower_id, followee_id) with both directions indexed (graph service).
- Feed cache: per-user list of the latest ~800 post IDs in Redis. 500M users x 800 x 8 bytes = 3.2 TB raw; keep only for active users, which shrinks it substantially.

HYBRID FAN-OUT
- Normal authors: fan-out on write. On publish, enqueue a job; workers fetch follower lists in pages and push post_id into each follower's feed list (LPUSH + LTRIM).
- Celebrities (followers above ~100k): do not fan out. At read time, merge the user's precomputed feed with recent posts from the celebrities they follow (pulled from per-author timelines, heavily cached).
- Inactive users: skip fan-out; rebuild their feed on login via fan-out on read.

READ PATH
- Get post IDs from feed cache, merge celebrity posts, hydrate posts and authors from caches in batch (multi-get), filter deleted/blocked, return.

PAGINATION
- Cursor based on post_id (time-sortable), not offset; "posts older than X" stays stable while new posts arrive at the head.

MEDIA
- Upload to object storage via pre-signed URLs, serve via CDN.

TRADE-OFFS
- Fan-out on write: fast reads, write amplification, wasted work for inactive followers.
- Fan-out on read: no amplification, but expensive reads touching hundreds of timelines.
- Ranking: a later stage scores candidate posts; the candidate generation above stays the same.

PITFALLS
- Deletes and unfollows: filter at read time rather than scrubbing every feed.
- Fan-out backlog during spikes: queue-based workers, prioritize active users.
- Hot keys for celebrity posts: replicate in cache, use local in-process caches.

title: Chat Messaging System
prompt:
Design a messaging app supporting one-to-one and group chats on mobile and web.

Functional requirements:
- Send and receive text messages in real time; groups up to 500 members.
- Message history synced across a user's devices.
- Delivery states: sent, delivered, read.
- Online/last-seen presence.
- Offline users receive messages when they reconnect, plus a push notification.

Scale:
- 200M daily active users, 50M concurrently connected at peak.
- 40B messages/day; average message 100 bytes.

Questions to answer:
1. How do clients maintain real-time connections and how do you route a message to the right server?
2. How do you guarantee per-conversation ordering and no message loss?
3. What storage model fits message history at this volume?
4. How does group delivery and presence scale?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 40B/day = ~460k msgs/s average, ~1M/s peak.
- Storage: 40B x ~200 bytes with metadata = 8 TB/day, ~3 PB/year before replication.
- 50M concurrent connections at ~100k per gateway node = ~500 gateway nodes.

CONNECTIONS
- Clients hold a persistent WebSocket (or MQTT) to a stateless-ish gateway tier.
- A session registry (Redis) maps user_id/device_id -> gateway node, updated on connect/disconnect with heartbeats.
- Gateways forward client sends to a chat service; chat service looks up recipients' gateways and pushes.

SEND FLOW
- Client sends {client_msg_id, conversation_id, body}.
- Chat service assigns a per-conversation monotonically increasing sequence number (e.g. via a counter in the conversation's shard) and persists the message, then ACKs the sender with the server ID and sequence.
- Fan-out to online recipients via their gateways; for offline devices, send a push notification.
- client_msg_id makes retries idempotent.

ORDERING AND NO LOSS
- Order within a conversation by sequence number; no global ordering needed.
- Each device tracks the last sequence it has seen per conversation. On reconnect, it asks for messages after that sequence. This sync-based design means a dropped push is never a lost message.

STORAGE
- Wide-column store (Cassandra/ScyllaDB/HBase): partition key conversation_id (bucketed by time for huge groups), clustering key sequence. Efficient "latest N messages" and range queries.
- Per-user inbox table listing conversations ordered by last activity.
- Media in object storage plus CDN.

GROUPS
- Fan-out on write to member devices for groups up to 500; message stored once, delivery pointers per member.
- Read receipts in groups aggregated (store per-member last-read sequence rather than per-message rows).

PRESENCE
- Heartbeat-based, stored in Redis with TTL. Publish presence changes only to users who currently have the chat open or are in the contact list and online; throttle updates. Presence is best-effort.

PITFALLS
- Relying on push delivery alone without a sync protocol.
- Using timestamps from clients for ordering.
- Hot partitions for very large groups; bucket partitions by time.
- End-to-end encryption changes the design: server stores ciphertext, group key management (sender keys) becomes a major component.

title: Search Autocomplete
prompt:
Design the query autocomplete for a large search engine: as the user types, show the top 10 suggested completions.

Functional requirements:
- Suggestions for any prefix, ranked by popularity, updated at least daily.
- Trending queries (breaking news) should surface within about 15 minutes.
- Filter offensive or blocked suggestions.
- Support multiple languages/locales.

Scale:
- 1B searches/day; average query 4 words, ~20 characters; a keystroke request is sent roughly every character after debounce.
- 100M distinct queries worth indexing.
- Latency target: under 50 ms p99 including network.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you compute popularity from query logs?
2. What data structure serves top-k completions for a prefix fast?
3. How do you distribute and update this index?
4. How do you blend in trending queries without a full rebuild?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 1B searches x ~6 suggestion requests (with debounce) = 6B requests/day = ~70k/s average, ~200k/s peak.
- 100M queries x ~30 bytes = 3 GB of strings; with precomputed top-k per node, index is tens of GB. Fits in memory across a modest cluster, replicated widely.

DATA COLLECTION
- Search logs flow into Kafka; a daily batch job (Spark) aggregates query counts with time decay (e.g. weighted last 30 days), normalizes (lowercase, trim), drops rare queries (privacy: require k distinct users) and blocklisted terms.

INDEX STRUCTURE
- Trie where every node stores the precomputed top 10 completions for that prefix. Lookup is O(prefix length) and no subtree traversal at query time.
- Memory-optimized alternatives: a sorted array of queries with binary search for the prefix range plus precomputed top-k; or FST (finite state transducer) as used by Lucene.
- Cap prefix depth (e.g. 20 chars); beyond that, fall back to search.

SERVING
- Autocomplete service holds the index in memory; shard by prefix range (or by first 2 chars, rebalanced by traffic) and replicate each shard many times.
- Cache top prefixes aggressively: one- and two-character prefixes are a tiny keyspace and serve a large share of traffic. Browser and CDN caching with short TTL.
- Client debounces (~100 ms), cancels stale requests, and caches results locally.

UPDATES
- Build new index offline, ship as an immutable snapshot, hot-swap on servers (blue/green). No in-place mutation.
- Trending: a streaming job (Flink) computes counts over sliding 5-15 minute windows and detects spikes vs baseline. A small trending index is merged with the main index at query time: final score = base score + boosted trending score.

PERSONALIZATION AND LOCALE
- Separate indexes per locale. Personal history blended on the client or via a small per-user store.

PITFALLS
- Updating the trie on every search; contention and inconsistent reads.
- Leaking private queries (names, phone numbers) through suggestions; require minimum distinct-user counts.
- Ignoring the spikiness of short prefixes when sharding by prefix.

title: Web Crawler
prompt:
Design a crawler that downloads web pages to feed a search index.

Functional requirements:
- Start from seed URLs, extract links, and keep discovering new pages.
- Respect robots.txt and per-site politeness (no more than one request every few seconds per host by default).
- Avoid storing duplicate content; recrawl pages based on how often they change.
- Store raw HTML for downstream indexing.

Scale:
- Crawl 1B pages per week; average page 100 KB.
- Tens of millions of distinct hosts.

Questions to answer:
1. What does the URL frontier look like, and how does it enforce politeness and priority together?
2. How do you detect already-seen URLs and duplicate content at this scale?
3. How do you distribute the crawl across machines?
4. What traps and failure modes must you guard against?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 1B pages/week = ~1,650 pages/s; aim for 3-5k/s headroom.
- Bandwidth: 1,650 x 100 KB = ~165 MB/s (~1.3 Gbps).
- Storage: 100 TB/week raw HTML, ~20-30 TB compressed.
- Seen-URL set: tens of billions of URLs over time.

COMPONENTS
- URL frontier, fetchers, DNS resolver cache, robots.txt cache, parser/link extractor, URL normalizer and filter, seen-URL store, content dedup, content store (object storage / HDFS in WARC files), recrawl scheduler.

FRONTIER (Mercator-style)
- Front queues by priority (PageRank-ish score, freshness need, site importance).
- Back queues: one per host, each fetcher thread owns hosts. A heap keyed by "next allowed fetch time" per host enforces the crawl delay.
- Frontier mostly on disk with in-memory buffers at the head and tail of each queue.

DISTRIBUTION
- Partition by hash of hostname to crawler nodes. All URLs for a host land on the same node, so politeness is enforced locally without coordination. Links discovered for other hosts are forwarded to their owning node in batches.
- Consistent hashing to rebalance when nodes join or leave.

DEDUP
- URL normalization (lowercase host, strip fragments, sort query params, remove session IDs).
- Seen URLs: Bloom filter in memory for fast negative checks backed by a persistent KV store (RocksDB) for exact checks.
- Exact content dup: hash of body. Near-dup: SimHash with Hamming distance threshold.

RECRAWL
- Track change frequency per page; schedule next fetch adaptively (frequently changing news pages hourly, static pages monthly). Use conditional GET (ETag / If-Modified-Since).

ROBUSTNESS
- Spider traps: cap URL length and path depth, cap pages per host per crawl, detect repeating path segments, calendar pages.
- Timeouts, max page size, content-type filtering.
- Cache DNS; DNS is a classic bottleneck.
- Checkpoint frontier state so node failures do not lose work.

PITFALLS
- Global politeness via a central lock service; partition by host instead.
- Re-fetching robots.txt per request; cache it per host with a TTL.
- Treating the crawler as BFS only; priority matters for quality.

title: Distributed Cache
prompt:
Design an in-memory distributed cache (in the spirit of Memcached/Redis Cluster) used by many backend services to offload a database.

Functional requirements:
- get, set with TTL, delete for string keys and binary values up to 1 MB.
- Horizontal scaling by adding nodes with minimal data movement.
- Survive single-node failures without a thundering herd on the database.

Scale:
- 10 TB of cached data; 5M operations/s at peak; read:write about 10:1.
- p99 latency under 1 ms within a data center.

Questions to answer:
1. How do clients find which node owns a key, and what happens when nodes are added or removed?
2. What eviction policy and memory management approach do you use?
3. Should you replicate, and how does that affect consistency with the database?
4. How do you deal with hot keys and cache stampedes?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 10 TB / ~100 GB usable RAM per node = ~100 primary nodes; with 1 replica each, ~200 nodes.
- 5M ops/s / 100 primaries = 50k ops/s per node, comfortable for an event-loop server.

PARTITIONING
- Consistent hashing with virtual nodes (hundreds per physical node) so adding/removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys and load spreads evenly.
- Alternative: fixed hash slots (Redis Cluster uses 16,384) mapped to nodes; rebalancing moves whole slots.
- Routing: smart client library holding the ring/slot map (fewest hops) or a proxy tier (simpler clients, extra hop). Config/membership served by a coordination service (etcd/ZooKeeper) or gossip.

MEMORY AND EVICTION
- LRU or approximated LRU (sample a few keys, evict the oldest), or LFU for skewed workloads.
- Slab allocator to avoid fragmentation; per-key overhead matters at billions of keys.
- TTL expiry: lazy on access plus periodic sampling.

REPLICATION AND CONSISTENCY
- Primary-replica per shard, async replication; failover promotes a replica. A cache tolerates losing a few recent writes.
- Cache-aside pattern: read cache, on miss read DB and populate. On writes, update DB then delete the cache key (not set it) to reduce races.
- Remaining race: a stale reader can repopulate an old value after delete; mitigate with short TTLs, versioned values, or lease tokens (Facebook memcache leases).

HOT KEYS AND STAMPEDES
- Request coalescing / single-flight: only one request per key goes to the DB on miss; others wait.
- Leases or "stale-while-revalidate": serve the stale value while one worker refreshes.
- Jittered TTLs so many keys do not expire simultaneously.
- Hot keys: replicate the key to several nodes with a suffix (key_1 .. key_N) and read randomly, or use a small in-process L1 cache.

FAILURE HANDLING
- On node loss, its keys miss; without care the DB gets hammered. Use replicas, gradual warm-up, and a "gutter" pool that temporarily absorbs failed node traffic.

PITFALLS
- Modulo hashing (hash mod N): adding one node remaps almost every key.
- Treating the cache as a source of truth.
- Large values causing latency spikes; cap value size and compress.

title: Metrics and Monitoring Platform
prompt:
Build an internal monitoring system (think Prometheus/Datadog) that collects time-series metrics from all services, stores them, supports dashboards, and fires alerts.

Functional requirements:
- Ingest metrics as (name, tags/labels, timestamp, value) at 10-second resolution.
- Query with aggregation over tags and time (e.g. p99 latency by service over 7 days).
- Alerting rules evaluated every minute with notifications.
- Retain raw data 15 days, downsampled data for 1 year.

Scale:
- 100k hosts, each emitting 1,000 series every 10 s.
- 500 concurrent dashboard users; 50k alert rules.

Questions to answer:
1. What is the ingestion rate and how do you collect it (push vs pull)?
2. How do you store time-series data compactly and query it quickly?
3. How do you handle high-cardinality tags?
4. How do you make alerting reliable even when the monitoring system is degraded?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Active series: 100k x 1,000 = 100M.
- Ingest: 100M / 10 s = 10M data points/s.
- Raw size with Gorilla-style compression ~1.5 bytes/point: 10M x 1.5 = 15 MB/s, ~1.3 TB/day, ~20 TB for 15 days per replica.
- Uncompressed (16 bytes/point) would be ~14 TB/day, so compression is essential.

COLLECTION
- Pull (Prometheus scraping) gives built-in liveness detection and server-side rate control; push (agents to a gateway) works better for short-lived jobs and across network boundaries. At this scale: local agent on each host aggregates and pushes batches to an ingestion tier.
- Ingestion tier writes to Kafka for buffering, then to storage nodes.

STORAGE
- Series identified by hash of name+sorted labels; partition by series ID across storage nodes, replicated (RF=3 or 2 with Kafka replay).
- In-memory head block for recent 2 hours, then flushed to immutable compressed blocks (delta-of-delta timestamps, XOR floats) on disk/object storage.
- Inverted index from label=value to series IDs for query selection.
- Downsampling job compacts old blocks into 5-min and 1-hour rollups (min, max, sum, count) for long retention.

QUERY
- Query frontend splits by time range, caches results for completed intervals, and fans out to storage shards; shards do partial aggregation, frontend merges.
- Choose resolution automatically based on range (raw for last day, rollups for months).

CARDINALITY
- Tags like user_id or request_id explode series counts and memory. Enforce per-tenant series limits, reject or drop offending labels, and expose cardinality dashboards. Push high-cardinality data to logs/traces instead.

ALERTING
- Rule evaluators sharded by rule ID, reading recent data from the hot tier.
- Alert manager dedups, groups, silences, and routes to on-call.
- Meta-monitoring: an independent minimal system watches the monitoring system; dead man's switch alerts that fire when the pipeline stops.

TRADE-OFFS
- Percentiles cannot be averaged across hosts; store histograms or sketches (t-digest, DDSketch) to aggregate correctly.
- Ingest favors availability: drop or delay points rather than block producers.

PITFALLS
- Using a general-purpose RDBMS row per point.
- Late or out-of-order samples; allow a bounded out-of-order window.
- Alerting on the same cluster you are trying to alert about with no external fallback.

title: File Sync Service (Dropbox-like)
prompt:
Design a cloud file storage and sync service with desktop and mobile clients.

Functional requirements:
- Users upload files and folders; changes sync automatically to all their devices.
- Share folders with other users with edit or view permission.
- Version history for 30 days; restore deleted files.
- Work offline and sync when back online; detect conflicting edits.

Scale:
- 100M users, 20M daily active; average user stores 10 GB.
- 1B file changes/day; files range from bytes to 50 GB.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you upload and store large files efficiently, especially when only part of a file changes?
2. How is metadata modeled, and how do clients learn about changes?
3. How do you resolve conflicting edits from two offline devices?
4. How do you scale and secure the storage layer?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Storage: 100M x 10 GB = 1 EB logical; dedup and compression reduce physical by maybe 30-50%.
- Metadata changes: 1B/day = ~12k/s, peaks ~50k/s.
- Upload bandwidth dominated by chunk transfers; delta sync reduces it greatly.

CHUNKING
- Split files into chunks (fixed 4 MB, or content-defined chunking with rolling hash so insertions do not shift every chunk boundary).
- Each chunk identified by SHA-256. Client asks server which hashes are missing and uploads only those: enables resumable uploads, delta sync, and cross-user dedup.
- Chunks stored in object storage (or a custom block store) keyed by hash, encrypted at rest.

METADATA MODEL
- namespaces (a user root or shared folder), each with a monotonically increasing journal.
- file entries: namespace_id, path, file_id, latest_version, is_deleted.
- versions: file_id, version, chunk_hash list, size, modified_by, timestamp.
- Sharded relational DB (by namespace_id) for transactional updates of a namespace's journal.

SYNC PROTOCOL
- Each client keeps a cursor per namespace (last journal sequence).
- Notification service: long-poll or WebSocket tells clients "namespace X changed"; client then pulls journal entries after its cursor and downloads missing chunks.
- Commit is a two-step: upload chunks first, then a metadata commit that references them. The file appears only after commit, so readers never see partial files.

CONFLICTS
- Commits carry the parent version. If server latest != parent, the commit is rejected; client saves its copy as "file (conflicted copy from Laptop)". Simple, predictable, no silent data loss. Merging content is not attempted for arbitrary files.

SHARING AND PERMISSIONS
- Shared folders are their own namespaces mounted into members' trees; ACLs checked on metadata and chunk access (chunks fetched via signed URLs).

SCALING AND DURABILITY
- Block storage with erasure coding across zones for durability (11 nines) at lower cost than 3x replication.
- Garbage collection: reference count chunks; delete unreferenced ones after version retention expires. Run carefully (mark and sweep with grace periods).
- Hot vs cold tiers for old versions.

PITFALLS
- Cross-user dedup can leak information (confirm someone has a file); limit to per-user dedup or use convergent encryption with care.
- Uploading whole files on every change.
- Clients polling the metadata DB directly instead of a notification fan-out.

title: Video Streaming Platform
prompt:
Design a video platform where creators upload videos and viewers stream them on any device.

Functional requirements:
- Upload videos up to 10 GB; process into multiple resolutions and formats.
- Adaptive bitrate playback that adjusts to network conditions; seeking.
- View counts, video metadata pages, and basic recommendations entry point.

Scale:
- 500k uploads/day, average 500 MB source.
- 200M daily viewers, 1B views/day, average 10 minutes watched at ~3 Mbps.

Questions to answer:
1. What does the upload and transcoding pipeline look like?
2. How is video delivered to viewers worldwide at this bandwidth?
3. How much storage and egress is required, and how do you control cost?
4. How do you count views accurately at this scale?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Uploads: 500k x 500 MB = 250 TB/day of source.
- Transcoded renditions (240p-4K, two codecs) roughly 1-2x source size: another ~250-500 TB/day.
- Egress: 1B views x 10 min x 3 Mbps = 1B x 225 MB = ~225 PB/day, average ~20 Tbps. Only a CDN with edge caches (including ISP-embedded boxes) can serve this.

UPLOAD
- Client requests an upload session; uploads directly to object storage via resumable, chunked pre-signed URLs.
- On completion, an event triggers the processing pipeline.

TRANSCODING PIPELINE
- Split source into segments (GOP-aligned, ~2-10 s) and transcode in parallel across a worker fleet (a DAG: validate, split, transcode per rendition, thumbnails, captions, content moderation, packaging).
- Output: HLS/DASH segments plus manifests per rendition. Codecs: H.264 for compatibility, VP9/AV1 for bandwidth savings on popular videos.
- Orchestrated by a workflow engine with retries; status stored in the video metadata DB. Video becomes public when the minimum rendition set is ready.

DELIVERY
- Player fetches the manifest, then segments from the CDN; ABR algorithm picks bitrate per segment based on throughput and buffer level.
- Popular content pre-positioned at edges; long tail served from regional origin shields to protect origin storage.
- Signed URLs/tokens for access control; DRM for premium content.

STORAGE COST
- Popularity follows a power law: transcode expensive codecs (AV1) only for videos above a view threshold.
- Move cold video renditions and sources to cheaper storage tiers; consider deleting rarely watched high renditions and re-transcoding on demand.

METADATA
- videos table (sharded SQL or KV), search index, comments in separate service; heavy caching for watch pages.

VIEW COUNTING
- Player sends heartbeat events to an ingestion endpoint, into Kafka; stream processor dedups (per user/session/video window), filters bots, and aggregates counts.
- Display counter in a sharded counter store updated in batches; eventual consistency is fine. Exact audited counts computed in batch for monetization.

PITFALLS
- Transcoding a whole long video on one machine.
- Serving video from application servers or origin directly.
- Synchronous counter increments in a single DB row per video (hot row on viral videos).

title: Ride-Hailing Dispatch and Matching
prompt:
Design the backend that matches riders with nearby drivers for a ride-hailing app.

Functional requirements:
- Drivers send their location periodically while online.
- A rider requests a ride; the system offers it to suitable nearby drivers, one or a few at a time, until one accepts.
- A driver must never be assigned two rides at once; a ride must not be accepted by two drivers.
- Riders see the assigned driver's live location until pickup.

Scale:
- 5M active drivers at peak globally, location update every 4 s.
- 1M ride requests/hour at peak; matching should complete within 10-30 seconds for most requests.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you ingest and index driver locations for fast nearby queries?
2. How does the matching and offer flow work, including timeouts and declines?
3. How do you guarantee one driver per ride and one ride per driver?
4. How do you partition the system geographically and handle a city-level outage?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Location updates: 5M / 4 s = 1.25M writes/s. Each ~100 bytes = 125 MB/s.
- Ride requests: 1M/hour = ~280/s, each triggering a nearby search and a few offers.
- Only current location must be hot; history goes to cheap storage for analytics.

LOCATION INDEX
- Geospatial cells: H3 hexagons or S2 cells / geohash at ~1 km resolution.
- In-memory store per region: cell_id -> set of available driver IDs, plus driver_id -> {lat, lng, cell, status, vehicle, ts}.
- On update, move the driver between cells if needed. Entries with stale timestamps (over ~30 s) are treated as offline.
- Nearby query: look up the rider's cell and its k-ring neighbors, filter by status/vehicle type, rank by ETA (from a routing service), not straight-line distance.
- Updates go through a gateway to a location service sharded by region/cell; they are lossy-tolerant (next update arrives in 4 s), so no durable write per update is needed on the hot path. Stream to Kafka for history.

MATCHING FLOW
- Ride request creates a ride record (state: REQUESTED) in a durable DB.
- Matcher gets candidates, sends an offer to the best driver with a 10-15 s timeout; on decline or timeout, offer to the next. Batched matching (collect requests for 1-2 s and solve an assignment problem per area) improves global efficiency.
- States: REQUESTED -> OFFERED -> ACCEPTED -> ARRIVING -> IN_PROGRESS -> COMPLETED / CANCELED, managed by a state machine with persisted transitions.

EXCLUSIVITY
- Driver lock: on offer, conditionally set driver state from AVAILABLE to OFFERED (compare-and-set) with a TTL; a driver can only hold one offer.
- Ride acceptance: conditional update "set driver_id = X where ride_id = R and state = OFFERED and offered_to = X". Only one acceptance can win; late accepts get a "ride no longer available" response.

GEO PARTITIONING
- Each city/region is served by its own cell of services and data (rides rarely cross regions), so failures are contained.
- Ride state replicated to a standby region; location index can be rebuilt from incoming updates within seconds.

LIVE TRACKING
- Rider subscribes over WebSocket to the assigned driver's location channel; the location service publishes updates to subscribers.

PITFALLS
- Writing every location update to a relational DB.
- Offering the same ride to many drivers simultaneously without exclusivity, causing double accepts.
- Ignoring supply/demand hot spots (airports, stadiums): those cells need splitting or dedicated shards.

title: Payments Ledger
prompt:
Design the core ledger for a payments company that moves money between user wallets, merchants, and external banks.

Functional requirements:
- Record every money movement as balanced double-entry transactions.
- Get the current balance of any account and its full transaction history.
- Transfers between internal accounts must be atomic; balances must never go negative unless an account allows overdraft.
- Integrate with external payment processors that may time out or respond late.
- Daily reconciliation with bank statements.

Scale:
- 50M accounts; 5k transactions/s peak, 100M transactions/day.
- Data retained for 7+ years for audit.

Questions to answer:
1. What is the data model for double-entry accounting, and how do you compute balances?
2. How do you make the payment APIs idempotent and safe under retries and timeouts?
3. How do you handle a transfer whose external leg has an unknown outcome?
4. How do you scale writes while keeping correctness, including hot accounts?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 100M txns/day, each with at least 2 entries: ~200M+ entries/day, ~70B/year. At ~200 bytes each: ~15 TB/year.
- 5k txns/s is modest for sharded SQL; correctness is the hard part, not throughput.

DATA MODEL
- accounts(account_id, type, currency, allow_negative, balance, version).
- transactions(txn_id, idempotency_key UNIQUE, type, status, created_at).
- entries(entry_id, txn_id, account_id, amount signed, currency). Invariant: entries of each txn sum to zero per currency.
- Entries are append-only and immutable. Corrections are new reversing transactions, never updates or deletes.
- Use integer minor units (cents), never floats.

BALANCES
- Source of truth is the sum of entries. Maintain a materialized balance on the account row updated in the same DB transaction as the entries, guarded by a check (balance + amount >= 0) or optimistic version.
- Periodic job verifies materialized balances against entry sums.

IDEMPOTENCY
- Every mutating API requires an idempotency key; stored with the request hash and the final response. Retries return the saved response; same key with a different payload is an error.

EXTERNAL LEGS
- Model as a state machine: PENDING -> SUBMITTED -> SUCCEEDED / FAILED. Funds first moved into a holding (suspense) account in the ledger.
- On timeout, the outcome is UNKNOWN: do not retry blindly with a new request. Retry with the same processor idempotency key, or query status; reconciliation resolves the rest.
- Use an outbox table written in the same DB transaction, with a relay publishing events to Kafka, so ledger state and downstream events never diverge.

SCALING
- Shard by account_id. Transfers within a shard are single DB transactions.
- Cross-shard transfers: avoid 2PC by moving through a clearing account per shard with a saga (debit A to clearing on shard 1, credit B from clearing on shard 2), each step idempotent, with compensating entries on failure. Balances stay consistent per shard; global invariant checked by reconciliation.
- Hot accounts (a big merchant receiving thousands of credits/s): split into sub-accounts and sum for balance, or batch credits asynchronously since credits cannot cause overdraft.

RECONCILIATION
- Daily job matches internal records against processor and bank files; mismatches create exceptions for ops review.

PITFALLS
- Updating a balance column without an entries trail.
- Floating point money.
- Distributed transactions across services without idempotency.
- Treating timeouts as failures and refunding while the payment actually succeeded.

title: Distributed Job Scheduler
prompt:
Design a platform that lets teams schedule jobs to run at specific times or on cron schedules (like a distributed cron / Airflow-lite).

Functional requirements:
- Register jobs with a cron expression or a one-time run time, a payload (container image or HTTP callback), timeout, and retry policy.
- Jobs run at their scheduled time within a few seconds of accuracy.
- A scheduled run should execute once; retries on failure per policy.
- Users can view run history, pause, and trigger jobs manually.
- Optional dependencies: job B runs after job A succeeds.

Scale:
- 10M registered jobs; up to 50k job runs starting in the same minute at peak (e.g. top of the hour).
- Job durations from seconds to hours.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you find jobs that are due without scanning all 10M every second?
2. How do you avoid double execution when scheduler nodes fail or network partitions occur?
3. How do workers pick up, heartbeat, and report on runs?
4. How do you handle the top-of-the-hour thundering herd?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- 50k runs in a minute = ~830/s spikes, much higher if all at second zero.
- Run history: assume 100M runs/day x 500 bytes = 50 GB/day.

DATA MODEL
- jobs(job_id, owner, schedule, payload, timeout, retry_policy, paused, next_run_at).
- runs(run_id, job_id, scheduled_time, attempt, status, worker_id, lease_expires_at, started_at, finished_at). Unique (job_id, scheduled_time) prevents duplicate run creation.

FINDING DUE JOBS
- Index on next_run_at. Partition jobs into N buckets (hash of job_id); each scheduler node owns a set of buckets (lease via etcd/ZooKeeper).
- Each scheduler polls its buckets every second for next_run_at <= now + lookahead, creates run rows, and enqueues them; then computes and stores the next next_run_at. Alternative: a hierarchical timing wheel in memory loaded with the next few minutes of jobs.

EXACTLY-ONCE (EFFECTIVELY)
- Run creation is idempotent via the unique (job_id, scheduled_time) constraint, so two schedulers racing for the same bucket after a failover cannot create duplicate runs.
- Execution is at-least-once: workers claim runs with a lease (conditional update status QUEUED -> RUNNING with lease_expires_at, owner). Workers heartbeat to extend the lease. If a lease expires, the run is re-queued.
- Pass a fencing token (attempt number) to the job so downstream systems can reject stale attempts. Job authors must still make handlers idempotent; true exactly-once side effects are not achievable in general.

WORKERS
- Pull model from a queue (Kafka/SQS) partitioned by priority/tenant; workers launch containers or call HTTP callbacks with timeout enforcement.
- Results written back to runs; retries scheduled with backoff by creating a new attempt with a future time.

THUNDERING HERD
- Pre-enqueue with lookahead so runs are ready to dispatch at the exact second.
- Allow jobs to declare a jitter window; spread non-critical jobs automatically.
- Per-tenant concurrency quotas so one team cannot starve others.
- Autoscale worker pools ahead of known peaks.

DEPENDENCIES
- DAG stored per workflow; on run success, a coordinator marks downstream nodes ready when all parents succeeded.

PITFALLS
- Single leader scheduler with no failover, or failover without fencing.
- Using local cron on many machines.
- Missed runs after downtime: define a catch-up policy (run once, run all, skip).
- Time zones and DST for cron expressions.

title: Distributed Lock Service
prompt:
Several teams need a shared service to acquire mutually exclusive locks across machines (e.g. only one worker processes a given account at a time, leader election for a scheduler).

Functional requirements:
- acquire(lock_name, ttl), release(lock_name), and renew for long-held locks.
- Optional blocking acquire with wait and fairness.
- A crashed client's lock must eventually be released.
- Protected resources must be safe even if a client pauses (GC, network) past its lease.

Scale:
- 100k distinct locks active, 20k acquire/release operations per second.
- The service must survive the loss of a node without granting a lock to two holders.

Questions to answer:
1. What backing store and consensus approach gives you safety?
2. How do leases and TTLs work, and why is a TTL alone not enough for correctness?
3. What are fencing tokens and how are they used?
4. How would you compare using a single Redis instance, Redlock, and etcd/ZooKeeper?
notes:
SAFETY VS EFFICIENCY
- Decide which lock you need. Efficiency locks (avoid duplicate work, occasional double execution is okay): Redis SET NX PX is fine. Correctness locks (double holders corrupt data): need consensus plus fencing.

DESIGN FOR CORRECTNESS
- Back the service with a Raft-based store (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul) on 3 or 5 nodes. Writes commit on a majority, so a minority partition cannot grant locks.
- 20k ops/s is manageable for a well-provisioned Raft cluster; shard lock namespaces across several independent Raft groups if needed.

API AND LEASES
- acquire: create key lock/{name} if absent, attached to a client session lease with TTL (e.g. 10 s). Returns success plus a fencing token.
- Client keeps the session alive with heartbeats. If heartbeats stop, the lease expires and all its keys are deleted.
- release: delete key only if owned (compare owner/revision).
- Blocking acquire: watch the key, or use sequential ephemeral nodes (ZooKeeper recipe) where each waiter watches only its predecessor: fair FIFO and avoids herd effects.

WHY TTL IS NOT ENOUGH
- A client can pause after acquiring (GC pause, VM freeze), its lease expires, another client acquires, then the first resumes and writes. Both believe they hold the lock.

FENCING TOKENS
- Each successful acquire returns a strictly increasing number (e.g. the etcd revision or ZooKeeper zxid).
- The protected resource (DB, storage) records the highest token seen and rejects writes with older tokens. This turns a stale holder into a harmless rejected write.
- Requires the resource to participate; if it cannot, you cannot get full safety from locking alone.

COMPARISON
- Single Redis: fast, simple, but failover with async replication can lose the lock key and grant it twice.
- Redlock (majority of independent Redis nodes): better availability, but relies on bounded clock drift and pauses; no native fencing token. Debated for correctness use.
- etcd/ZooKeeper: consensus-backed, linearizable, revision numbers usable as fencing tokens. Higher latency, but correct.

PITFALLS
- Releasing a lock you no longer own (delete without checking owner).
- TTL too short for the work; renew periodically and abort work if renewal fails.
- Using wall-clock comparisons across machines for lock validity.

title: Event Ticketing (No Overselling)
prompt:
Design a ticketing platform for concerts and sports where fans pick specific seats and pay.

Functional requirements:
- Browse events and see a live seat map with availability.
- Select up to 8 seats and hold them for 10 minutes while paying.
- Never sell the same seat twice; release holds when they expire or payment fails.
- Handle hugely popular on-sales fairly.

Scale:
- Typical events: a few thousand seats, low traffic.
- Hot on-sale: 60k-seat stadium, 2M users arrive in the first minute, 500k try to hold seats in the first few minutes.

Questions to answer:
1. How do you model seat inventory and implement holds without overselling?
2. How do you protect the system and keep things fair when 2M users arrive at once?
3. How do you integrate payment so a seat is not lost or double-sold if payment is slow or fails?
4. How do you keep the seat map reasonably fresh for millions of viewers?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Hot event: 60k seats but 2M users. Read load on the seat map is the dominant cost; write contention is on a small, fixed set of rows.
- Seat data for one event is tiny (60k rows); the issue is concurrency, not size.

DATA MODEL
- events(event_id, venue_id, on_sale_at, ...).
- seats(event_id, seat_id, section, price_tier, status AVAILABLE|HELD|SOLD, hold_id, hold_expires_at, version).
- holds(hold_id, user_id, event_id, seat_ids, expires_at, status).
- orders(order_id, hold_id UNIQUE, payment_id, status).

HOLDS WITHOUT OVERSELLING
- Atomic conditional update in a single transaction: UPDATE seats SET status=HELD, hold_id=?, hold_expires_at=now+10m WHERE event_id=? AND seat_id IN (...) AND (status='AVAILABLE' OR (status='HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now)). Succeeds only if the affected row count equals the number requested; otherwise roll back.
- All seats of one event live on one shard, so multi-seat holds are local transactions.
- Alternative for extreme throughput: an in-memory seat allocator per event (single-threaded actor or Redis Lua script) that serializes hold requests, backed by durable writes.
- Expiry is lazy (the WHERE clause treats expired holds as available) plus a sweeper to clean up.

VIRTUAL WAITING ROOM
- Before on-sale, users enter a queue served from CDN/edge with a static page; assign random positions to everyone who arrives before start time (fair, removes bot advantage of being first by milliseconds).
- Admit users in batches at the rate the inventory service can handle, issuing signed short-lived access tokens checked at the gateway.
- Bot defense: CAPTCHAs, per-account limits, verified fan programs.

PAYMENT
- Checkout creates an order with idempotency key tied to the hold. Charge via the payment provider.
- On success: transaction sets seats SOLD only if still held by this hold_id. If the hold expired and the seat was taken during a slow payment, refund automatically; better, extend the hold while payment is in progress (pending state) so this rarely occurs.
- On failure or timeout: keep status pending and query the provider before releasing; never release on an unknown outcome.

SEAT MAP FRESHNESS
- Serve section-level availability counts from a cache updated every few seconds; detailed seat map fetched per section.
- Push updates via WebSocket/SSE to admitted users only. The map can be slightly stale because the hold operation is the final check.

PITFALLS
- Check-then-update in two steps (read AVAILABLE, then write) without a conditional write or lock.
- Distributed locks per seat across many services instead of a single transactional owner.
- Letting all 2M users hit the inventory service directly.

title: Collaborative Document Editor
prompt:
Design a Google Docs-style editor where multiple people edit the same rich-text document simultaneously.

Functional requirements:
- Real-time co-editing; everyone converges to the same document state.
- Show collaborators' cursors and selections.
- Offline edits merge when the user reconnects.
- Full version history with the ability to restore; comments anchored to text.

Scale:
- 50M daily active users, 5M documents open concurrently.
- Most documents have 1-3 editors; some have up to 100 simultaneous editors and thousands of viewers.
- Edit operations: about 1 per second per active typist.

Questions to answer:
1. Operational transformation or CRDTs: how does each guarantee convergence, and which would you choose?
2. How do clients and servers exchange operations, and where is the authoritative order decided?
3. How are documents and history persisted efficiently?
4. How do you scale to millions of open documents and handle a very popular document?
notes:
ESTIMATES
- Assume 10M active typists x 1 op/s = 10M ops/s peak globally, batched by clients every ~100-200 ms into far fewer messages.
- Op log: ~50 bytes per op, 10M/s would be ~40 TB/day raw; compaction via snapshots is essential.

OT VS CRDT
- OT: clients send ops based on a known revision; the server transforms incoming ops against ops committed since that revision and assigns a total order. Simple data, needs a central sequencer per document. Proven (Google Docs).
- CRDT (RGA, Yjs, Automerge): each character/element has a unique ID; merges are commutative so any order converges. Works peer-to-peer and offline; costs metadata overhead (tombstones, IDs) and memory.
- Reasonable choice: server-centered OT, or a CRDT with a server relay for ordering and persistence. CRDT is stronger for offline-first.

PROTOCOL (OT, central sequencer)
- Client applies ops locally immediately (optimistic), keeps at most one outstanding batch, and sends {doc_id, base_revision, ops}.
- Document session server transforms against newer ops, assigns revision N+1, appends to the log, ACKs the sender, and broadcasts to other clients, who transform against their pending local ops.
- Cursors/presence are ephemeral messages, not persisted, throttled.

ROUTING
- Each open document is owned by exactly one session server (consistent hashing on doc_id with a lease in a coordination service). All editors connect, via WebSocket gateways, to that owner. Single owner makes ordering trivial and avoids cross-node coordination.
- On owner failure, a new owner takes the lease, loads the latest snapshot plus log tail, and clients resync from their last ACKed revision.

STORAGE
- Append-only op log per document (wide-column store keyed by doc_id, revision) plus periodic snapshots (every N ops) in object storage.
- Load = latest snapshot + replay ops after it. Version history = named snapshots plus the log.
- Comments anchored to stable positions (CRDT IDs or OT-transformed anchors).

POPULAR DOCUMENTS
- Separate editors from viewers: viewers subscribe via a fan-out tier (pub/sub) that relays committed ops, so the owner only handles editors.
- Batch broadcasts; cap simultaneous editors per document with graceful degradation to view mode.

PITFALLS
- Last-writer-wins on the whole document; loses edits.
- Using wall-clock timestamps to order concurrent ops.
- Unbounded op logs or CRDT tombstones without compaction.
- Permission changes must take effect on live sessions (revoke the connection).

title: Expression Tree with Box

Implement parallel_map, which applies a function to every input using a fixed pool of worker threads that communicate over std::sync::mpsc channels, and returns the results in the ORIGINAL input order.

Signature:
  pub fn parallel_map<F>(inputs: Vec<i64>, workers: usize, f: F) -> Vec<i64>
  where F: Fn(i64) -> i64 + Send + Sync + 'static

Requirements:
- Spawn exactly max(workers, 1) worker threads (not one per item).
- Send jobs to the workers as (index, value) pairs. A common pattern: one job channel whose Receiver is shared as Arc<Mutex<Receiver<(usize, i64)>>>, and one result channel that every worker holds a Sender clone of.
- Workers loop until the job channel is closed (recv returns Err), so drop the job Sender once all jobs are sent.
- Collect (index, result) pairs from the result channel and place each result at its index.
- Join all worker threads before returning.

Also implement count_workers_used, which runs the same pool on the inputs but returns how many DISTINCT worker threads processed at least one job (use thread::current().id()). It exists so the tests can check you really used a pool: it must never exceed max(workers, 1).

Example:
  parallel_map(vec![1, 2, 3, 4], 2, |x| x * x) -> [1, 4, 9, 16]

title: Dijkstra Shortest Paths
prompt:
Implement Dijkstra's algorithm on a directed graph with non-negative u64 edge weights.

shortest_paths(n, edges, src) -> Vec<Option<u64>>
- n: number of nodes, labeled 0..n
- edges: slice of (from, to, weight)
- returns dist where dist[v] is Some(shortest distance from src to v), or None if v is unreachable. dist[src] is Some(0).

Use std::collections::BinaryHeap. It is a max-heap, so wrap entries in std::cmp::Reverse (or implement Ord on a custom struct) to pop the smallest distance first. Skip stale heap entries.

Also implement shortest_path(n, edges, src, dst) -> Option<(u64, Vec<usize>)> returning the total distance and the node sequence from src to dst (inclusive), or None if unreachable. If several shortest paths exist, any one is accepted. For src == dst, return Some((0, vec![src])).

The graph may contain parallel edges and self-loops. Expected complexity: O((V + E) log V).

Example:
  edges = [(0,1,4), (0,2,1), (2,1,2), (1,3,1)]
  shortest_paths(4, &edges, 0) -> [Some(0), Some(3), Some(1), Some(4)]
  shortest_path(4, &edges, 0, 3) -> Some((4, [0, 2, 1, 3]))

title: Generic LRU Cache
prompt:
Implement a generic least-recently-used cache LruCache<K, V> with a fixed capacity.

- new(capacity): create an empty cache. A capacity of 0 means nothing is ever stored.
- get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<&V>: return the value and mark the key as most recently used.
- put(&mut self, key, value) -> Option<(K, V)>: insert or update. Updating an existing key replaces its value, marks it most recently used, and returns None. Inserting a new key into a full cache first evicts the least recently used entry and returns it as Some((k, v)). With capacity 0, put returns Some((key, value)) immediately (the item is "evicted" straight away).
- peek(&self, key) -> Option<&V>: like get but does NOT change recency.
- len(&self) -> usize
- keys_mru(&self) -> Vec<K>: keys from most recently used to least recently used.

Bounds: K: Eq + Hash + Clone. Use std::collections::HashMap plus a recency structure such as a VecDeque<K>. An O(capacity) update of the recency order is acceptable for this exercise; an O(1) design (e.g. index-based doubly linked list in a Vec) is a stretch goal.

Example (capacity 2):
  put(1,"a"); put(2,"b"); get(&1) -> Some("a"); put(3,"c") -> Some((2,"b")); keys_mru() -> [3, 1]

title: Generic Binary Search Tree
prompt:
Implement a generic binary search tree using Option<Box<Node<T>>> for child links.

Bst<T: Ord> methods:
- new() -> empty tree
- insert(&mut self, value: T) -> bool: insert value; return false (and do nothing) if it was already present.
- contains(&self, value: &T) -> bool
- len(&self) -> usize: number of stored values
- height(&self) -> usize: number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path (empty tree = 0, single node = 1)
- min(&self) -> Option<&T> and max(&self) -> Option<&T>
- in_order(&self) -> Vec<&T>: values in ascending order
- range_count(&self, lo: &T, hi: &T) -> usize: how many stored values v satisfy lo <= v <= hi. Prune subtrees that cannot contain values in range.

Tip: insertion can walk down with a mutable cursor: let mut cur = &mut self.root; while let Some(node) = cur { ... cur = &mut node.left; } — be careful with the borrow checker, a recursive helper is also fine. Note that a degenerate (sorted-input) tree can be thousands of nodes deep; recursion to depth ~3000 is fine with the default test thread stack.

Example:
  insert 5, 3, 8, 1, 4 -> in_order = [1, 3, 4, 5, 8], height = 3, range_count(&2, &5) = 3

title: Task Scheduler: Topological Sort
prompt:
You are given tasks and dependencies. Each dependency (a, b) means task a must run BEFORE task b. Produce an execution order.

topo_order(tasks: &[&str], deps: &[(&str, &str)]) -> Result<Vec<String>, TopoError>

Rules:
- Use Kahn's algorithm. Whenever several tasks are ready (in-degree 0), always pick the alphabetically smallest one next, so the output is deterministic. A BTreeSet works well as the ready queue.
- If a dependency mentions a task not in `tasks`, return Err(TopoError::UnknownTask(name)) for the first such name encountered scanning deps in order (check a before b within a pair).
- If the graph has a cycle, return Err(TopoError::Cycle(remaining)) where remaining is the sorted list of tasks that could not be scheduled.
- Duplicate dependency pairs should be treated as one edge. A self-dependency (a, a) is a cycle.

Example:
  tasks = ["cook", "eat", "shop", "wash"]
  deps  = [("shop","cook"), ("cook","eat"), ("wash","cook")]
  -> Ok(["shop", "wash", "cook", "eat"])
